Disruption details

British Airways flight BA707 from Larnaca International Airport to London Heathrow Airport was diverted to Gatwick Airport after a technical problem delayed departure by more than 3 hours. The flight was due to reach Heathrow on 19 October 2026, but the delay pushed its expected arrival beyond the airport's nighttime operating window.

For passengers, this meant a lengthy wait in Cyprus followed by an arrival at a different airport shortly after midnight. If you were on board, your journey didn't end at the London airport you'd booked to fly into.

The technical issue was identified before boarding. It was fixed before passengers boarded the Airbus A320, but the time spent resolving it left the aircraft unable to reach Heathrow within its normal arrival hours.

The aircraft flew directly toward Gatwick. Heathrow's nighttime restrictions limit routine flights to reduce noise. Routine arrivals aren't permitted between 10:40 pm and 5:05 am, while routine departures aren't permitted between 10:50 pm and 6:00 am.

Some exceptional flights can receive permission to operate during those hours. However, a late-running service can't assume it'll be allowed to land after the normal operating window closes.

British Airways apologized and said it arranged onward transportation to help passengers continue their journeys after landing at Gatwick in West Sussex. The airline said its teams worked to get customers on their way as quickly as possible.

If you traveled on BA707, you may be entitled to compensation under EC 261, the EU's air passenger rights rules, or the UK's equivalent, UK 261. The flight departed from Cyprus for the United Kingdom, and the initial delay was caused by a technical problem within the airline's control.

Your eligibility depends on the circumstances of your journey, including how late you reached your final destination. A departure delay of more than 3 hours doesn't, on its own, confirm that compensation is owed.

Disruption overview

An unexpected air traffic control staffing issue at Kirkwall Airport disrupted Loganair connections with Edinburgh Airport and Aberdeen Airport on 28 and 29 October 2026.

The tower closed from 6:00 pm on Wednesday, with further brief closures planned for Thursday and cancellations affecting evening services and the next morning's Kirkwall–Aberdeen flight.

Loganair should arrange rebooking, welfare support, and overnight accommodation where needed. The airline has added a Thursday afternoon Edinburgh–Kirkwall return service departing Edinburgh at 3:30 pm.

Disruption details

Loganair flights between Orkney, Edinburgh, and Aberdeen were canceled after air traffic control at Kirkwall Airport closed early on Wednesday, 28 October 2026. The closure started at 6:00 pm because of unforeseen staffing issues, with further short closures planned for Thursday, 29 October.

For affected passengers, this meant rearranged journeys and, in some cases, an overnight stay. If you're traveling on these routes, Loganair should contact affected customers directly and arrange alternative flights where possible.

The disruption affected a limited number of services linking Kirkwall Airport with Edinburgh Airport and Aberdeen Airport. Canceled services included:

The evening Edinburgh–Kirkwall return service on Wednesday, 28 October.

The Aberdeen–Kirkwall flight on Wednesday, 28 October.

The morning Kirkwall–Aberdeen service on Thursday, 29 October.

Highlands and Islands Airport Limited, which manages the air traffic control tower, linked the closure to unexpected staffing problems. The operator apologized for the disruption and advised passengers to contact their airline for the latest travel information.

Loganair said the issue was outside its control. The airline is providing welfare support and overnight accommodation where needed, as well as moving customers onto earlier flights where possible.

To help passengers complete their journeys, Loganair also announced an additional Edinburgh–Kirkwall return service for Thursday afternoon. The extra flight is scheduled to leave Edinburgh at 3:30 pm on 29 October.

Compensation under UK 261 is unlikely for these cancellations because the air traffic control staffing issue was outside Loganair's control. That doesn't mean passengers are without support: if your flight is canceled, you can ask about rebooking or a refund if you no longer wish to travel.

Care and assistance can also include food and refreshments during a long wait, plus accommodation if you're left away from home overnight. Contact Loganair to confirm your arrangements and the support you need.
